qs.q: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with right shoulder pain, Horner syndrome, and weakness of the right hand. A computed tomography scan reveals a mass at the superior sulcus of the right lung. Which anatomic structure's involvement explains the Horner syndrome?
o: D. Phrenic nerve descending along pericardium
B. Lower trunk of the brachial plexus network
C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve within thorax
A. Cervical sympathetic chain and ganglion
E. Vagus nerve trunk within superior mediastinum
qs.e: Pancoast tumors in the superior sulcus can compress the cervical sympathetic chain, resulting in classic ipsilateral Horner syndrome.
qs.s: Weekly Pathology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis. Computed tomography demonstrates a 5 cm pericolic abscess adjacent to the sigmoid colon without diffuse intraperitoneal free air. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
qs.e: Percutaneous image-guided drainage with intravenous antibiotics is the initial treatment of choice for a localized intra-abdominal abscess greater than 3 cm. Surgical intervention is reserved for diffuse peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, or failure of radiologic drainage.
qs.s: Acute Abdomen: Clinical Assessment and Classification: MCQs

qs.q: A 70-year-old man presents with acute colicky abdominal pain, absolute constipation, and abdominal distension. A computed tomography scan shows a 'bird-beak' sign and a massively dilated sigmoid colon. What is the definitive management step to reduce recurrence after initial decompression?
qs.e: Sigmoid volvulus has a high recurrence rate after conservative endoscopic detorsion, necessitating elective sigmoid resection once the bowel is prepared.
qs.s: Weekly Year 4: Surgery Exam - October 30, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A 7-year-old child is hit by a car and sustains a closed head injury. A computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a skull fracture where a bone fragment is displaced inward. Under which specific condition is surgical elevation indicated for this type of fracture?
o: The child develops a transient period of amnesia
The fracture line crosses a meningeal vascular groove
The fracture is located over the temporal bone
The depression exceeds the thickness of the skull
qs.e: Surgical elevation of a depressed skull fracture is indicated if the depression is more than the thickness of the skull or twice the thickness of the table, if it is compound, or if there are neurological signs.
qs.s: Head Injury: Assessment, Intracranial Haematomas and Management of: MCQs

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman with a history of tuberous sclerosis is found to have a 5 cm asymptomatic solid renal lesion that shows macroscopic fat density on computed tomography. What is the most likely diagnosis?
qs.e: Angiomyolipomas are benign renal lesions characterised by the presence of fat on CT and are strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis. They carry a risk of bleeding when larger than 4 cm, unlike malignant renal carcinomas.
qs.s: Renal Masses and Renal Cell Carcinoma: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with long-standing nodular goitre develops sudden thyrotoxicosis after receiving an iodine-containing contrast agent for a computed tomography scan. What is the recognized pathophysiological term for this phenomenon?
qs.e: The Jod-Basedow effect refers to iodine-induced hyperthyroidism occurring in patients with autonomous thyroid tissue such as a multinodular goitre. Conversely, the Wolff-Chaikoff effect is the temporary inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis by high doses of iodide.
qs.s: Thyroid Disorders: Thyrotoxicosis, Graves' Disease, Thyroid Storm and: MCQs

qs.q: An elderly patient experiences a minor fall and develops a progressive headache and confusion two weeks later. Computed tomography reveals a crescent-shaped collection of blood over the lateral cerebral hemisphere. Which vessel was most likely disrupted?
qs.e: Elderly patients are at high risk for subdural hematomas due to brain atrophy stretching the fragile bridging veins. The middle meningeal artery is implicated in epidural hematomas, which present with a more acute arterial course.
qs.s: CNS Trauma Neuropathology: Fractures, Concussion & CTE: MCQs

qs.q: An elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism presents with a slow-onset, progressive neurological decline weeks after a minor head trauma. Computed tomography of the brain shows a crescent-shaped collection of blood that crosses suture lines. What is the ruptured vascular source?
qs.e: Subdural haematomas are caused by the rupture of bridging veins, resulting in a low-pressure venous bleed that appears as a crescent-shaped lesion on CT and can cross suture lines. Epidural haematomas involve arterial bleeding from the middle meningeal artery.

ai.title: Computed Tomography in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: CT provides cross‑sectional images that reveal anatomy and pathology not seen on plain radiographs. In low‑resource settings it guides urgent decisions when other modalities are unavailable.

sections.p: CT uses rotating X‑ray beams and detectors to create axial images of the body, reconstructed into slices. It is ordered when detailed anatomy is needed beyond plain X‑ray.
b: Provides 1‑5 mm slice thickness
Can be performed with or without intravenous contrast

sections.p: CT findings are graded by established radiologic scores (e.g., CT severity index for COVID‑19, Bosniak classification for renal cysts). Staging informs treatment urgency.
b: CT severity index ≥ 15 → high risk of respiratory failure
Bosniak III/IV → consider surgical excision

sections.p: The indication for CT varies by organ. In East Africa the most common reasons are:
b: Pulmonary infection or TB with cavitation
Abdominal pain from appendicitis, perforated ulcer, or intestinal obstruction
Head trauma from road‑traffic accidents
Suspected malaria‑related cerebral edema

sections.p: Patients are usually symptomatic (fever, pain, altered consciousness) and require imaging to confirm or exclude serious pathology.
b: Fever + cough → CT chest for TB or empyema
Acute abdomen → CT abdomen/pelvis for perforation
Head injury with GCS < 13 → CT brain for bleed

sections.p: CT is selected after bedside assessment and basic labs. When contrast is unavailable, non‑contrast scans still give valuable information.

t.b: Detects cavitary TB, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion; a cavity with thick wall suggests TB.
Answers if there is perforation, abscess, or vascular injury; extravasated contrast indicates leak.
Identifies intracranial bleed, mass, or edema; hyperdense crescent = subdural hematoma.
Use non‑contrast to look for high‑density blood, calcifications, or air; if still inconclusive, arrange transfer.

sections.p: CT itself can cause contrast nephropathy and radiation injury; recognise when the benefit outweighs risk.
b: Acute kidney injury before IV contrast → avoid contrast
Pregnancy → use non‑contrast or defer unless life‑threatening
Allergy to iodinated contrast → pre‑medicate or use non‑contrast

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause identified on CT, then provide supportive care. Choose drugs that address the pathology without worsening imaging findings.
b: TB cavity → start standard anti‑TB regimen; avoid steroids unless massive airway obstruction
Perforated ulcer → IV antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) and surgical consult; avoid NSAIDs
Intracranial bleed → reverse coagulopathy, control blood pressure; avoid anticoagulants

sections.p: Repeat CT only when clinical change occurs; use ultrasound or plain X‑ray for routine monitoring to limit radiation.
b: Post‑TB: repeat CT at 6 months if symptoms persist
After abdominal surgery: ultrasound for fluid collections
Low‑dose CT for lung cancer screening in high‑risk smokers

sections.p: CT is frequently mixed up with MRI or plain radiography.
b: MRI gives better soft‑tissue contrast but is less available
Chest X‑ray is quicker but misses early parenchymal disease

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls are common in low‑resource settings.
b: Non‑contrast CT may miss small bowel ischemia; consider clinical signs
Contrast enhancement can be absent in renal failure, mimicking non‑vascular lesions

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness with suspected intracranial bleed
Severe abdominal pain with signs of peritonitis
High‑grade fever with respiratory distress and possible empyema

faq.q: Can CT replace X‑ray in diagnosing TB?
faq.a: CT is more sensitive for cavitation and mediastinal nodes, but X‑ray remains first line where CT is unavailable.

faq.q: Is contrast always needed for abdominal CT?
faq.a: Contrast improves detection of leak and vascular injury; if contraindicated, non‑contrast can still identify perforation by free air.

faq.q: What is the safest way to limit radiation in children?
faq.a: Use low‑dose protocols, limit scanned area, and consider ultrasound first when feasible.

exam: A 30‑year‑old man with HIV presents with chronic cough and weight loss – which imaging modality best confirms pulmonary TB and why — CT chest shows cavitary lesions with thick walls, more sensitive than X‑ray for early disease.

A child with head injury and GCS = 12 is unstable – what is your next step and what CT finding would change management — Perform non‑contrast CT; a subdural hematoma >10 mm thickness mandates neurosurgical evacuation.

A patient with acute abdomen and raised urea is allergic to iodinated contrast – how would you still obtain useful imaging — Use non‑contrast CT to look for free air and fluid; if still equivocal, arrange ultrasound or transfer for MRI.

You see a peripheral lung nodule on CT in a non‑smoker; what are the key features that differentiate benign from malignant — Smooth borders, <6 mm size, and calcification suggest benign; spiculated margins and growth on follow‑up suggest malignancy.

During a CT scan for suspected perforated ulcer, the radiologist reports ‘no contrast extravasation’ but the patient remains febrile — What else should you consider and how to act — Look for retroperitoneal air on plain film; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and surgical review.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester needs imaging for suspected appendicitis — which modality is preferred and why — Ultrasound first; if inconclusive, low‑dose non‑contrast CT is acceptable because fetal radiation dose is below harmful thresholds.

Explain why high‑resolution CT (HRCT) is preferred over conventional CT for evaluating asbestosis — HRCT visualises interlobular septal thickening and honeycombing with thin slices, increasing sensitivity for early disease.

A patient with renal failure requires CT for trauma — how do you modify the study to avoid worsening kidney function — Perform non‑contrast CT; if vascular injury is suspected, use low‑osmolar contrast with pre‑hydration and monitor creatinine.
